lesson.title: Building Up: When Simple Substances Combine
lesson.summary: A synthesis reaction combines two or more simpler substances into a single, more complex product, following the general pattern A + B forms AB.
lesson.body:
Among the five reaction families introduced in Reaction Types Overview, synthesis reactions are the simplest to picture: two or more reactants come together and combine into a single product, following the general form A + B -> AB. Nothing is left over as a separate substance, and nothing besides the reactants goes in; everything that started as multiple pieces ends up bonded into one. This is the pattern behind forming many common compounds directly from their elements, and it is often the most direct route from raw elements to a useful compound.

A vivid, easily observed example is the burning of magnesium metal in air. Magnesium ribbon, when ignited, reacts with the oxygen gas around it and burns with an intensely bright white light, which is exactly why magnesium has historically been used in flares, fireworks, and old photographic flashbulbs. The two separate reactants, solid magnesium metal and oxygen gas, combine into a single new solid product, magnesium oxide, a white powder left behind after the flame goes out. Written with full state symbols: 2 Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2 MgO(s).

Check the balance atom by atom. The left side has 2 Mg atoms from the 2 in front of Mg, and 2 O atoms from the single O2 molecule. The right side has 2 MgO formula units, contributing 2 magnesium atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. Both sides show 2 Mg and 2 O, so the equation is balanced. This is a textbook synthesis reaction: two separate elemental reactants entering, and exactly one compound product leaving, with every atom accounted for on both sides.

It is worth noticing the mirror-image relationship this pattern has with the next chapter's topic. A synthesis reaction combines simple substances into a complex one; a decomposition reaction takes that same complex substance and breaks it back apart into simpler pieces. In fact, the same pair of substances often can be pushed in either direction depending on the conditions supplied: water can be formed by burning hydrogen in oxygen, a synthesis reaction, or it can be split back into hydrogen and oxygen gas by running an electric current through it, a decomposition reaction. Keeping that reversibility in mind makes the next chapter's pattern easier to recognize, since it is quite literally synthesis read backward.
